evaluated.name: PriceyGoodwillRollup
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive revenue-multiple firms with rising goodwill should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: A high price-to-sales multiple reflects optimistic expectations about future growth. When paired with large goodwill increases, that optimism may be tied to acquisition-led expansion rather than organic value creation, a setting prone to overpayment and later disappointment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SalesValueHiringDiscipline
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that are cheap on sales and also restrain headcount growth should earn higher returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Sales yield identifies firms priced cheaply relative to their revenue base. The bottleneck structure requires both cheapness and hiring discipline, penalizing firms where low valuation is accompanied by aggressive labor expansion that may pressure margins.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: HarvestingCashFlowValue
evaluated.hypothesis: High operating-cash-flow-yield firms should outperform when capex intensity is falling relative to their own recent sales-scaled history.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids a simple cash-flow-to-price crossed with low capex level by requiring a within-firm capex downshift rather than static underinvestment. The economic idea is that cheap cash generators entering a harvesting or capital-discipline phase may be revalued, while cheap firms still increasing capital intensity are more likely to remain value traps.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyInventoryOverbuild
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms with rising inventory-to-sales should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: A high price-to-sales multiple requires confidence that growth will convert cleanly into revenue and margins. Inventory accumulation relative to sales indicates possible demand overestimation or aggressive production, so the interaction targets overvalued growth stories where investment discipline is already weakening.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CapitalAdjustedEbitdaYield
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms with high operating cash profitability relative to both market price and installed tangible capital should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces dividend-yield payer effects and the stacked capex/debt composite with a single valuation ratio adjusted for capital intensity. A high value identifies firms that are cheap while requiring relatively little tangible asset base to generate EBITDA, consistent with underappreciated capital-efficient operators.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EarningsValuePPEEfficiencyTrend
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap earnings firms with improving sales productivity from tangible capital should earn higher future returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The signal requires both low price relative to earnings and a positive trend in sales generated per unit of net PPE. This focuses on cheap firms where the installed capital base is becoming more productive, rather than simply rewarding low asset growth or low capex levels.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyOverhiringSalesGap
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms whose employee growth exceeds sales growth should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: A high price-to-sales multiple implies expectations for scalable revenue growth. When headcount expands faster than sales, operating leverage may be deteriorating just as the stock is priced for growth, indicating an overvalued and undisciplined expansion plan.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapPredictableCapexYield
evaluated.hypothesis: High operating-cash-flow-yield firms with predictable capex intensity should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids simply rewarding low capex or adding capex to a market-value denominator; the investment leg instead measures stability of reinvestment needs. Cheap cash generators with stable capex-to-sales are more likely to produce durable free cash flow, while industry ranking helps reduce exposure to broad HML and CMA structure.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapitalProductivityFade
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive sales-multiple firms with declining operating productivity of gross PPE should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This shifts away from the simple expensive-plus-rising-investment template and focuses on whether the installed capital base is becoming less productive. A high price-to-sales multiple is vulnerable when EBITDA generated per unit of gross PPE is trending down, because valuation optimism is not being supported by capital productivity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapOrganicSalesNoAcquisition
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap revenue firms whose sales growth is not heavily acquisition-funded should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the inventory-overbuild mechanism with an organic-growth discipline mechanism. The signal favors firms priced cheaply relative to revenue where sales growth exceeds recent acquisition intensity, distinguishing underappreciated organic operators from firms buying top-line growth.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EbitdaValueMarginalPPEPayoff
evaluated.hypothesis: High EBITDA-yield firms whose EBITDA growth exceeds fixed-asset growth should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids intangible and goodwill balance-sheet changes, where amortization and accounting effects can obscure investment discipline. The interaction targets cheap operating-profit firms with evidence that incremental tangible investment is paying off rather than merely expanding the asset base.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapexCashBurn
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms whose capex exceeds operating cash generation should earn lower future returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not simply high capex intensity; it measures whether investment demand is internally funded or creates a cash-flow deficit. The interaction is most concerning for firms priced at high sales multiples, where investors may be overpaying for growth that consumes rather than generates cash.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NormalizedAfterCapexYield
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that are cheap after covering a normalized capex burden should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids dividing by capex, so near-zero capex firms do not mechanically dominate the ranking. The signal compares market price to operating earnings remaining after a smoothed reinvestment requirement, capturing valuation only when cash production survives investment needs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapInventoryReleaseGrowth
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms that are growing sales while releasing inventory capital should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the prior cash-flow-yield template with a sales-valuation condition and an operational test that inventory is being freed without sacrificing revenue growth. Industry ranking helps avoid simply rewarding sectors with structurally low inventories.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCashBurnAcquirer
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms making acquisitions while generating weak operating cash flow should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This targets acquisition discipline through internal funding capacity rather than comparing acquisition intensity to noisy revenue growth. The interaction is most bearish when investors pay a high revenue multiple for firms buying assets despite poor cash-generation economics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueCapexDecel
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms with decelerating capex intensity should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids the explosive scaling problem from dividing operating metrics by price-to-sales and instead asks whether cash-valued firms are becoming more restrained in capital deployment. The mechanism is underappreciated optionality: cash on the balance sheet is more valuable when management is not accelerating reinvestment demands.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyLossMakingHiring
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms expanding headcount while profitability is weak should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids a noisy trend in cash flow per employee and instead measures explicit labor expansion interacting with poor current economics. Hiring is most suspect when the firm is priced at a high sales multiple but lacks earnings margins to support the growth story.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashFundedCapexValue
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich firms priced cheaply that can cover capex from operating cash flow should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Prior evidence favored cash-valued firms with capex discipline, so this tests whether the key mechanism is investment self-funding rather than merely capex deceleration. The signal should identify firms where balance-sheet cash is valuable because ongoing investment does not consume incremental external capital.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CheapDepreciatedAssetYield
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap EBITDA-yield firms generating profits from an older depreciated asset base should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: A low net-PPE-to-gross-PPE ratio can indicate mature installed capacity that no longer requires aggressive recent investment. When such firms are also cheap on EBITDA yield, the market may underappreciate the cash-generating power of already-paid-for assets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueLaborLeverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms with sales growing faster than headcount should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This shifts the labor-discipline idea away from plain sales-to-price, which previously produced poor FF5 alpha, and toward cheap balance-sheet optionality. Sales growth exceeding employee growth indicates operating leverage without aggressive labor investment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapexCashDrawdown
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms with accelerating capex intensity and cash-balance drawdowns should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This extends the successful capex-cash-burn direction by focusing on balance-sheet funding strain rather than only current operating cash flow. A high sales multiple is most vulnerable when investment is accelerating while cash reserves are being consumed.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyInventoryFundingStrain
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms that are simultaneously building inventory and generating weak operating cash flow should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: The nested MIN structure makes the stress condition monotonic: the signal is high only when valuation is expensive, inventory is rising, and cash generation is weak. Inventory liquidation or strong cash flow no longer incorrectly receives a high stress score, so the expression better captures working-capital strain in overvalued growth firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyFreshCapacityUnderuse
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms with relatively new tangible capacity and deteriorating sales utilization of net PPE should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids treating profitable firms with newer assets as attractive or unattractive solely because of asset newness. The signal is bearish only when fresh capacity is paired with declining utilization, indicating that recent investment is not yet supporting the sales base implied by a high valuation multiple.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueInventoryReleaseFCF
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that are releasing inventory while generating free cash flow should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Prior inventory-release ideas had strong cross-sectional evidence but weak FF5 alpha when anchored on sales-to-price. This version anchors on the better-performing cash-value leg and requires inventory discipline to coincide with internally funded operations, distinguishing real working-capital efficiency from distressed sales contraction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueNoDilution
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that are not issuing equity should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Balance-sheet cash is more valuable to outside shareholders when management is not simultaneously diluting them to finance expansion. The interaction separates underpriced cash optionality from firms whose cash balances may be transient proceeds of external financing.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyDilutiveCapexDeficit
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms with capex funding deficits financed through equity issuance should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: PriceyCapexCashBurn worked well, and this tests whether the most overvalued subset is where the investment shortfall requires external equity capital. The nested MIN keeps the interpretation monotonic: the signal is high only when valuation is rich, investment exceeds operating cash generation, and dilution is present.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyHiringCashBurnGate
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms expanding headcount while burning operating cash should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Earlier labor short signals had useful portfolio evidence but were weakened by sign-flipping products or noisy productivity trends. This monotonic gate identifies firms priced for scalable growth where labor investment is rising before the business model generates cash.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashCapexRunwayValue
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich firms priced cheaply should outperform when their cash balance is large relative to recent cumulative capex needs.
evaluated.reasoning: This fixes the stock-flow issue by comparing cash to a multi-year cumulative capex claim rather than subtracting an annual flow from a balance-sheet stock. The bounded runway ratio reduces domination by plain cash-to-price and identifies firms where cash optionality is less likely to be consumed by ongoing reinvestment requirements.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapacityAheadOfDemand
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms expanding both labor and tangible capacity while sales growth is weak should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the inventory-cash-drawdown variant with a distinct capacity-before-demand mechanism. The nested gate is monotonic and only scores firms highly when valuation is rich, investment is broad-based across employees and fixed assets, and contemporaneous sales do not justify the expansion.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: HarvestingOldAssetCashValue
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms with depreciated asset bases and positive after-capex cash generation should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: The old-asset mechanism is most attractive when mature capacity is still producing free cash flow rather than simply reflecting underinvestment or asset shrinkage. Conditioning asset vintage on cash-to-price and after-capex funding discipline targets firms harvesting already-paid-for assets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AcquisitionRestraintCashValue
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that avoid acquisition spending should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Cash balances are more valuable to shareholders when management is not rapidly consuming them on acquisitions. This tests a disciplined-capital-allocation channel distinct from capex restraint: underpriced cash optionality should be strongest when the firm is not pursuing acquisitive empire building.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyDebtFundedCapexDeficit
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms with capex funding deficits financed through rising debt should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Prior negative-side evidence favored expensive firms whose investment exceeded operating cash generation. This version asks whether the deficit is being financed through balance-sheet leverage, a distinct funding channel from equity issuance and a potential warning that growth expectations are being sustained by borrowing.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NetCashCapexCutWithGrowth
evaluated.hypothesis: Net-cash-rich firms priced cheaply should outperform when they reduce capex intensity without sacrificing sales growth.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids recombining the prior cash-runway and no-dilution signals and instead tests whether capex restraint is disciplined rather than distress-driven. The signal is high only when the market undervalues net cash, capex-to-sales is falling, and sales are still growing.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyDebtFundedAcquirer
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms funding acquisition activity with rising debt should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the repeated acquisition-plus-cash-burn construction with a financing-discipline mechanism. A rich revenue multiple is most vulnerable when acquisitive growth is supported by leverage expansion, suggesting investors may be overpaying for externally financed growth.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapexDeficitNoBuffer
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms whose capex exceeds operating cash flow and that lack cash buffers should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the redundant asset-vintage leg and focuses on liquidity fragility around investment commitments. The signal is high only when valuation is rich, investment is not internally funded, and the balance sheet has little cash capacity to absorb the shortfall.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueRunwayImprovement
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms whose cash runway relative to recent capex needs is improving should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids mixing stock and flow units by using a bounded cash-to-cash-plus-cumulative-capex ratio, then looks for improvement in that runway. The mechanism is that cash optionality becomes more valuable when reinvestment demands are becoming easier to cover.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyTotalInvestmentCashDrain
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms whose combined capex and inventory investment exceeds operating cash flow should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This aggregates tangible investment and working-capital absorption into one monotonic cash-drain measure, avoiding sign-flipping products. A rich sales multiple is most fragile when growth consumes cash through both capital spending and inventory buildup.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValuePostCapexPeak
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform when current capex intensity has fallen meaningfully below its own recent peak.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the smoothed free-cash-flow-margin duplicate with an investment-cycle mechanism: cash is most valuable after a firm exits a heavy reinvestment phase. The within-firm distance from peak capex avoids simply rewarding low-capex industries and focuses on firms moving from expansion toward harvest.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueBroadInvestmentRestraint
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform when neither organic balance-sheet growth nor acquisition spending is aggressive.
evaluated.reasoning: This fixes the incoherent acquisition adjustment by penalizing acquisition intensity rather than subtracting it from asset growth. The MAX gate treats broad asset expansion and acquisitive expansion as alternative forms of investment aggressiveness, so the signal is high only when cheap cash optionality is paired with genuinely restrained capital deployment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyLeveredIntangibleBuild
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms building intangible assets while increasing leverage should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This moves away from the repeated capex-deficit/no-buffer structure and tests a distinct balance-sheet expansion channel. A rich sales multiple is especially vulnerable when growth is supported by levered intangible accumulation, where valuation optimism may rest on hard-to-verify assets financed with debt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyEquityIssuedCashHoard
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms issuing equity and accumulating cash should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids recombining employee growth with equity issuance and instead targets market-timing behavior: firms may issue stock when valuations are rich and park proceeds rather than deploy them productively. The interaction is bearish because shareholder dilution is occurring at high valuation without evidence of disciplined investment use.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueTotalInvestmentPeakExit
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform after combined capex and inventory investment falls below its own recent peak.
evaluated.reasoning: The strongest prior positive evidence came from cash-valued firms exiting high capex phases. This version broadens the investment cycle to include working-capital absorption, identifying firms moving from expansion toward harvest across both fixed capital and inventory.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueCapacityPruningGrowth
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that shrink tangible capacity while still growing sales should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This distinguishes disciplined capacity pruning from distress-driven asset contraction by requiring sales growth to remain positive. The interaction captures firms whose market value underprices cash while management improves capital efficiency by generating more revenue from a smaller fixed-asset base.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapexBurdenLowMargin
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms with high capex burdens and weak EBITDA margins should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: A high sales multiple is hard to justify when the business requires heavy capital spending but has poor operating margins. The monotonic gate avoids sign-flipping products and targets firms where reinvestment intensity is not supported by current unit economics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyShareholderFinancedInventoryBuild
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms building inventory while issuing equity should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Inventory accumulation is more concerning when it is financed through shareholder dilution rather than internal cash generation. The signal targets rich-multiple firms where capital markets are funding working-capital expansion before demand has clearly validated the growth story.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueAssetSaleHarvest
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that shrink gross tangible capacity while increasing cash net of external financing should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the weak capex-volatility duplicate with an asset-harvesting mechanism: management is actively releasing capital from the installed asset base. Using gross PPE decline reduces depreciation noise, while cash growth net of equity and debt financing helps distinguish genuine divestiture or internal harvest from newly raised capital.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyDebtFundedInventoryGlut
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms building inventory with debt while sales growth is weak should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids the criticized capex-deficit-plus-low-cash mashup and tests a distinct working-capital financing failure. The signal is high only when a rich sales multiple coincides with inventory accumulation, borrowing, and weak demand, indicating a growth story being financed ahead of validated sales.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueCapexCutMarginGain
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms cutting capex intensity while margins improve should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Capex cuts can be distress signals, so this conditions investment restraint on improving operating margins. The signal targets disciplined harvest rather than underinvestment: firms are cheap on cash, spending less per dollar of sales, and seeing better unit economics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapexMarginErosion
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms increasing capex intensity while EBITDA margins deteriorate should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: A high sales multiple requires confidence that reinvestment will scale profitably. Rising capex-to-sales paired with margin erosion suggests the opposite: capital demands are increasing while unit economics are weakening.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyInventoryMarginErosion
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms accumulating inventory while EBITDA margins deteriorate should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Inventory buildup is most concerning when it coincides with weakening margins, because it may signal discounting pressure, demand shortfalls, or production ahead of sales. For firms already priced at rich sales multiples, this interaction points to growth expectations becoming harder to justify.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueCapexCutDeleveraging
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that reduce capex intensity while paying down debt should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the runway-denominator tweak with a de-risking mechanism: cheap cash is more valuable when management is simultaneously lowering reinvestment intensity and reducing balance-sheet claims. The interaction aims to identify disciplined capital allocators moving from expansion funding toward balance-sheet repair.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueTrueAcquisitionExit
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform when they have a real history of acquisition spending but current acquisition intensity has fallen sharply.
evaluated.reasoning: The added prior-acquisition gate prevents never-acquirers from being pooled with genuine acquisition exits. The signal is strongest for firms where investors may still discount past dealmaking, but management has stopped consuming cash on acquisitions.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyIntangibleNoSalesValidation
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms increasing intangible-asset intensity without sales growth validation should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This moves away from another hiring-plus-profitability variant and instead tests whether hard-to-verify intangible investment is being capitalized before demand is evident. A high sales multiple is vulnerable when intangible assets are growing but the top line is weakening, suggesting the growth narrative may be overcapitalized.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapexCutCashFlowDistress
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms cutting capex while operating cash-flow margins deteriorate should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Capex restraint is not always good; for expensive firms it may signal a broken growth story if cash generation is also weakening. This distinguishes disciplined harvest from distress-driven investment cuts that contradict the valuation embedded in a high sales multiple.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueUtilizationHarvest
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform when existing fixed assets are highly utilized relative to history while capex intensity is low relative to history.
evaluated.reasoning: This avoids recombining the prior capex-peak and margin-gain winners and instead measures whether installed capital is doing more work without renewed reinvestment. The within-firm rank spread distinguishes disciplined harvesting from simple industry-level low capex.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueInventoryLeanGrowth
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that grow sales without proportional inventory growth should outperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the inventory-release-plus-cash-generation overlap with an inventory-scalability mechanism. The investment leg rewards firms where demand is expanding but working-capital investment is not keeping pace, reducing the risk that the signal merely captures liquidation or distress.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashValueAssetBackedAcquirer
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms making acquisitions should outperform when deal activity is not accompanied by large goodwill buildup.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests a different acquisition-discipline mechanism from acquisition exit: the firm is acquiring, but the deals appear more asset-backed and less goodwill-heavy. The explicit acquisition-intensity gate prevents never-acquirers from being pooled with genuinely disciplined acquirers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyCapexDeficitShortDebt
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms whose capex exceeds operating cash flow and that carry high short-term debt should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the mechanical investment-drain-plus-margin blend with a financing-fragility mechanism. A high sales multiple is especially vulnerable when investment is not internally funded and near-term debt claims may constrain continued growth financing.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PriceyIntangibleAccrualGrowth
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms increasing intangible-asset intensity while earnings exceed operating cash flow should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This fixes the cash-flow inconsistency by treating intangible growth as a capitalization/accrual-quality issue rather than a literal cash outflow. The signal is bearish when rich valuation coincides with hard-to-verify asset buildup and profits that are not well supported by cash generation.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: EarningsYieldAssetEfficiencyDecel

considered.reasoning: Earnings yield alone can be misleading if profits require increasingly heavy asset deployment. This signal favors cheap firms where assets per dollar of sales are decelerating, suggesting improving investment discipline or operating efficiency.

considered.name: NormalizedAfterCapexYield
considered.hypothesis: Firms that are cheap after covering a normalized capex burden should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids dividing by capex, so near-zero capex firms do not mechanically dominate the ranking. The signal compares market price to operating earnings remaining after a smoothed reinvestment requirement, capturing valuation only when cash production survives investment needs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapInventoryReleaseGrowth
considered.hypothesis: Cheap firms that are growing sales while releasing inventory capital should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the prior cash-flow-yield template with a sales-valuation condition and an operational test that inventory is being freed without sacrificing revenue growth. Industry ranking helps avoid simply rewarding sectors with structurally low inventories.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyCashBurnAcquirer
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms making acquisitions while generating weak operating cash flow should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This targets acquisition discipline through internal funding capacity rather than comparing acquisition intensity to noisy revenue growth. The interaction is most bearish when investors pay a high revenue multiple for firms buying assets despite poor cash-generation economics.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueCapexDecel
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms with decelerating capex intensity should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids the explosive scaling problem from dividing operating metrics by price-to-sales and instead asks whether cash-valued firms are becoming more restrained in capital deployment. The mechanism is underappreciated optionality: cash on the balance sheet is more valuable when management is not accelerating reinvestment demands.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyLossMakingHiring
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms expanding headcount while profitability is weak should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids a noisy trend in cash flow per employee and instead measures explicit labor expansion interacting with poor current economics. Hiring is most suspect when the firm is priced at a high sales multiple but lacks earnings margins to support the growth story.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashFundedCapexValue
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich firms priced cheaply that can cover capex from operating cash flow should outperform.
considered.reasoning: Prior evidence favored cash-valued firms with capex discipline, so this tests whether the key mechanism is investment self-funding rather than merely capex deceleration. The signal should identify firms where balance-sheet cash is valuable because ongoing investment does not consume incremental external capital.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CheapDepreciatedAssetYield
considered.hypothesis: Cheap EBITDA-yield firms generating profits from an older depreciated asset base should outperform.
considered.reasoning: A low net-PPE-to-gross-PPE ratio can indicate mature installed capacity that no longer requires aggressive recent investment. When such firms are also cheap on EBITDA yield, the market may underappreciate the cash-generating power of already-paid-for assets.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueLaborLeverage
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms with sales growing faster than headcount should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This shifts the labor-discipline idea away from plain sales-to-price, which previously produced poor FF5 alpha, and toward cheap balance-sheet optionality. Sales growth exceeding employee growth indicates operating leverage without aggressive labor investment.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyCapexCashDrawdown
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms with accelerating capex intensity and cash-balance drawdowns should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This extends the successful capex-cash-burn direction by focusing on balance-sheet funding strain rather than only current operating cash flow. A high sales multiple is most vulnerable when investment is accelerating while cash reserves are being consumed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyInventoryFundingStrain
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms that are simultaneously building inventory and generating weak operating cash flow should underperform.
considered.reasoning: The nested MIN structure makes the stress condition monotonic: the signal is high only when valuation is expensive, inventory is rising, and cash generation is weak. Inventory liquidation or strong cash flow no longer incorrectly receives a high stress score, so the expression better captures working-capital strain in overvalued growth firms.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyFreshCapacityUnderuse
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms with relatively new tangible capacity and deteriorating sales utilization of net PPE should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids treating profitable firms with newer assets as attractive or unattractive solely because of asset newness. The signal is bearish only when fresh capacity is paired with declining utilization, indicating that recent investment is not yet supporting the sales base implied by a high valuation multiple.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueInventoryReleaseFCF
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that are releasing inventory while generating free cash flow should outperform.
considered.reasoning: Prior inventory-release ideas had strong cross-sectional evidence but weak FF5 alpha when anchored on sales-to-price. This version anchors on the better-performing cash-value leg and requires inventory discipline to coincide with internally funded operations, distinguishing real working-capital efficiency from distressed sales contraction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueNoDilution
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that are not issuing equity should outperform.
considered.reasoning: Balance-sheet cash is more valuable to outside shareholders when management is not simultaneously diluting them to finance expansion. The interaction separates underpriced cash optionality from firms whose cash balances may be transient proceeds of external financing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyDilutiveCapexDeficit
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms with capex funding deficits financed through equity issuance should underperform.
considered.reasoning: PriceyCapexCashBurn worked well, and this tests whether the most overvalued subset is where the investment shortfall requires external equity capital. The nested MIN keeps the interpretation monotonic: the signal is high only when valuation is rich, investment exceeds operating cash generation, and dilution is present.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyHiringCashBurnGate
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms expanding headcount while burning operating cash should underperform.
considered.reasoning: Earlier labor short signals had useful portfolio evidence but were weakened by sign-flipping products or noisy productivity trends. This monotonic gate identifies firms priced for scalable growth where labor investment is rising before the business model generates cash.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashCapexRunwayValue
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich firms priced cheaply should outperform when their cash balance is large relative to recent cumulative capex needs.
considered.reasoning: This fixes the stock-flow issue by comparing cash to a multi-year cumulative capex claim rather than subtracting an annual flow from a balance-sheet stock. The bounded runway ratio reduces domination by plain cash-to-price and identifies firms where cash optionality is less likely to be consumed by ongoing reinvestment requirements.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyCapacityAheadOfDemand
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms expanding both labor and tangible capacity while sales growth is weak should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the inventory-cash-drawdown variant with a distinct capacity-before-demand mechanism. The nested gate is monotonic and only scores firms highly when valuation is rich, investment is broad-based across employees and fixed assets, and contemporaneous sales do not justify the expansion.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: HarvestingOldAssetCashValue
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms with depreciated asset bases and positive after-capex cash generation should outperform.
considered.reasoning: The old-asset mechanism is most attractive when mature capacity is still producing free cash flow rather than simply reflecting underinvestment or asset shrinkage. Conditioning asset vintage on cash-to-price and after-capex funding discipline targets firms harvesting already-paid-for assets.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AcquisitionRestraintCashValue
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that avoid acquisition spending should outperform.
considered.reasoning: Cash balances are more valuable to shareholders when management is not rapidly consuming them on acquisitions. This tests a disciplined-capital-allocation channel distinct from capex restraint: underpriced cash optionality should be strongest when the firm is not pursuing acquisitive empire building.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyDebtFundedCapexDeficit
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms with capex funding deficits financed through rising debt should underperform.
considered.reasoning: Prior negative-side evidence favored expensive firms whose investment exceeded operating cash generation. This version asks whether the deficit is being financed through balance-sheet leverage, a distinct funding channel from equity issuance and a potential warning that growth expectations are being sustained by borrowing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NetCashCapexCutWithGrowth
considered.hypothesis: Net-cash-rich firms priced cheaply should outperform when they reduce capex intensity without sacrificing sales growth.
considered.reasoning: This avoids recombining the prior cash-runway and no-dilution signals and instead tests whether capex restraint is disciplined rather than distress-driven. The signal is high only when the market undervalues net cash, capex-to-sales is falling, and sales are still growing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyDebtFundedAcquirer
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms funding acquisition activity with rising debt should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the repeated acquisition-plus-cash-burn construction with a financing-discipline mechanism. A rich revenue multiple is most vulnerable when acquisitive growth is supported by leverage expansion, suggesting investors may be overpaying for externally financed growth.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyCapexDeficitNoBuffer
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms whose capex exceeds operating cash flow and that lack cash buffers should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This drops the redundant asset-vintage leg and focuses on liquidity fragility around investment commitments. The signal is high only when valuation is rich, investment is not internally funded, and the balance sheet has little cash capacity to absorb the shortfall.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueRunwayImprovement
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms whose cash runway relative to recent capex needs is improving should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids mixing stock and flow units by using a bounded cash-to-cash-plus-cumulative-capex ratio, then looks for improvement in that runway. The mechanism is that cash optionality becomes more valuable when reinvestment demands are becoming easier to cover.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyTotalInvestmentCashDrain
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms whose combined capex and inventory investment exceeds operating cash flow should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This aggregates tangible investment and working-capital absorption into one monotonic cash-drain measure, avoiding sign-flipping products. A rich sales multiple is most fragile when growth consumes cash through both capital spending and inventory buildup.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValuePostCapexPeak
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform when current capex intensity has fallen meaningfully below its own recent peak.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the smoothed free-cash-flow-margin duplicate with an investment-cycle mechanism: cash is most valuable after a firm exits a heavy reinvestment phase. The within-firm distance from peak capex avoids simply rewarding low-capex industries and focuses on firms moving from expansion toward harvest.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueBroadInvestmentRestraint
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform when neither organic balance-sheet growth nor acquisition spending is aggressive.
considered.reasoning: This fixes the incoherent acquisition adjustment by penalizing acquisition intensity rather than subtracting it from asset growth. The MAX gate treats broad asset expansion and acquisitive expansion as alternative forms of investment aggressiveness, so the signal is high only when cheap cash optionality is paired with genuinely restrained capital deployment.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyLeveredIntangibleBuild
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms building intangible assets while increasing leverage should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This moves away from the repeated capex-deficit/no-buffer structure and tests a distinct balance-sheet expansion channel. A rich sales multiple is especially vulnerable when growth is supported by levered intangible accumulation, where valuation optimism may rest on hard-to-verify assets financed with debt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyEquityIssuedCashHoard
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms issuing equity and accumulating cash should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids recombining employee growth with equity issuance and instead targets market-timing behavior: firms may issue stock when valuations are rich and park proceeds rather than deploy them productively. The interaction is bearish because shareholder dilution is occurring at high valuation without evidence of disciplined investment use.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueTotalInvestmentPeakExit
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform after combined capex and inventory investment falls below its own recent peak.
considered.reasoning: The strongest prior positive evidence came from cash-valued firms exiting high capex phases. This version broadens the investment cycle to include working-capital absorption, identifying firms moving from expansion toward harvest across both fixed capital and inventory.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueCapacityPruningGrowth
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that shrink tangible capacity while still growing sales should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This distinguishes disciplined capacity pruning from distress-driven asset contraction by requiring sales growth to remain positive. The interaction captures firms whose market value underprices cash while management improves capital efficiency by generating more revenue from a smaller fixed-asset base.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyCapexBurdenLowMargin
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms with high capex burdens and weak EBITDA margins should underperform.
considered.reasoning: A high sales multiple is hard to justify when the business requires heavy capital spending but has poor operating margins. The monotonic gate avoids sign-flipping products and targets firms where reinvestment intensity is not supported by current unit economics.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyShareholderFinancedInventoryBuild
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms building inventory while issuing equity should underperform.
considered.reasoning: Inventory accumulation is more concerning when it is financed through shareholder dilution rather than internal cash generation. The signal targets rich-multiple firms where capital markets are funding working-capital expansion before demand has clearly validated the growth story.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueAssetSaleHarvest
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that shrink gross tangible capacity while increasing cash net of external financing should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the weak capex-volatility duplicate with an asset-harvesting mechanism: management is actively releasing capital from the installed asset base. Using gross PPE decline reduces depreciation noise, while cash growth net of equity and debt financing helps distinguish genuine divestiture or internal harvest from newly raised capital.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyDebtFundedInventoryGlut
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms building inventory with debt while sales growth is weak should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids the criticized capex-deficit-plus-low-cash mashup and tests a distinct working-capital financing failure. The signal is high only when a rich sales multiple coincides with inventory accumulation, borrowing, and weak demand, indicating a growth story being financed ahead of validated sales.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueCapexCutMarginGain
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms cutting capex intensity while margins improve should outperform.
considered.reasoning: Capex cuts can be distress signals, so this conditions investment restraint on improving operating margins. The signal targets disciplined harvest rather than underinvestment: firms are cheap on cash, spending less per dollar of sales, and seeing better unit economics.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyCapexMarginErosion
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms increasing capex intensity while EBITDA margins deteriorate should underperform.
considered.reasoning: A high sales multiple requires confidence that reinvestment will scale profitably. Rising capex-to-sales paired with margin erosion suggests the opposite: capital demands are increasing while unit economics are weakening.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyInventoryMarginErosion
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms accumulating inventory while EBITDA margins deteriorate should underperform.
considered.reasoning: Inventory buildup is most concerning when it coincides with weakening margins, because it may signal discounting pressure, demand shortfalls, or production ahead of sales. For firms already priced at rich sales multiples, this interaction points to growth expectations becoming harder to justify.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueCapexCutDeleveraging
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that reduce capex intensity while paying down debt should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the runway-denominator tweak with a de-risking mechanism: cheap cash is more valuable when management is simultaneously lowering reinvestment intensity and reducing balance-sheet claims. The interaction aims to identify disciplined capital allocators moving from expansion funding toward balance-sheet repair.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueTrueAcquisitionExit
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform when they have a real history of acquisition spending but current acquisition intensity has fallen sharply.
considered.reasoning: The added prior-acquisition gate prevents never-acquirers from being pooled with genuine acquisition exits. The signal is strongest for firms where investors may still discount past dealmaking, but management has stopped consuming cash on acquisitions.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyIntangibleNoSalesValidation
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms increasing intangible-asset intensity without sales growth validation should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This moves away from another hiring-plus-profitability variant and instead tests whether hard-to-verify intangible investment is being capitalized before demand is evident. A high sales multiple is vulnerable when intangible assets are growing but the top line is weakening, suggesting the growth narrative may be overcapitalized.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyCapexCutCashFlowDistress
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms cutting capex while operating cash-flow margins deteriorate should underperform.
considered.reasoning: Capex restraint is not always good; for expensive firms it may signal a broken growth story if cash generation is also weakening. This distinguishes disciplined harvest from distress-driven investment cuts that contradict the valuation embedded in a high sales multiple.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueUtilizationHarvest
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms should outperform when existing fixed assets are highly utilized relative to history while capex intensity is low relative to history.
considered.reasoning: This avoids recombining the prior capex-peak and margin-gain winners and instead measures whether installed capital is doing more work without renewed reinvestment. The within-firm rank spread distinguishes disciplined harvesting from simple industry-level low capex.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueInventoryLeanGrowth
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms that grow sales without proportional inventory growth should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the inventory-release-plus-cash-generation overlap with an inventory-scalability mechanism. The investment leg rewards firms where demand is expanding but working-capital investment is not keeping pace, reducing the risk that the signal merely captures liquidation or distress.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashValueAssetBackedAcquirer
considered.hypothesis: Cash-rich cheap firms making acquisitions should outperform when deal activity is not accompanied by large goodwill buildup.
considered.reasoning: This tests a different acquisition-discipline mechanism from acquisition exit: the firm is acquiring, but the deals appear more asset-backed and less goodwill-heavy. The explicit acquisition-intensity gate prevents never-acquirers from being pooled with genuinely disciplined acquirers.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyCapexDeficitShortDebt
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms whose capex exceeds operating cash flow and that carry high short-term debt should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the mechanical investment-drain-plus-margin blend with a financing-fragility mechanism. A high sales multiple is especially vulnerable when investment is not internally funded and near-term debt claims may constrain continued growth financing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PriceyIntangibleAccrualGrowth
considered.hypothesis: Expensive firms increasing intangible-asset intensity while earnings exceed operating cash flow should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This fixes the cash-flow inconsistency by treating intangible growth as a capitalization/accrual-quality issue rather than a literal cash outflow. The signal is bearish when rich valuation coincides with hard-to-verify asset buildup and profits that are not well supported by cash generation.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: This is a straightforward crossing of two canonical published anomalies — cash-flow-to-price (Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny) and capital investment intensity (Titman-Wei-Xie) — and as a value×investment composite it is close to spanned by HML and CMA, so a meaningful FF5 alpha is unlikely.

The earnings-yield leg is textbook Basu, but the second-difference in asset intensity (a turnover *acceleration* rather than a level or growth) is a genuinely less-traveled construction whose sign is internally consistent with the hypothesis, though negative-`ib` firms and the noisiness of a second difference of an annual ratio will hurt precision.

Market-to-book interacted with equity issuance is essentially the published market-timing/net-share-issuance literature (Baker-Wurgler, Pontiff-Woodgate, Daniel-Titman) restated, and both legs are already close to FF5 factor exposures.

Conditioning acquirer-style goodwill growth on an expensive price-to-sales multiple is a reasonably distinctive framing of acquisition overpayment rather than a direct rediscovery, but `gdwl` is missing or flat for a large share of firms, so expect degenerate rank ties and coverage-driven instability in the short leg.

This stacks three well-documented effects (dividend yield, capex intensity, external debt financing) into one composite, and because non-payers pile up at a dividend yield of exactly zero the first rank leg is largely a payer/non-payer dummy rather than a value measure.

Both legs are individually known (Barbee's sales-price ratio; the employee-growth anomaly of Bazdresch-Belo-Lin), but the conjunctive MIN bottleneck is a substantively different functional form from the usual multiplicative composite and is internally consistent with the stated hypothesis, with `emp` sparsity and annual staleness the main risks.

Because market cap dominates three years of capex for the vast majority of firms, this is numerically almost identical to plain sales-to-price (a classic published value anomaly) and structurally the same "add a capital stock to the market-value denominator" trick already tested as CapitalAdjustedEbitdaYield in the archive.

The conjunction of earnings yield with a within-firm trend in sales-per-unit-of-net-PPE is a coherent and reasonably novel "cheap plus improving capital productivity" construct not yet in the archive, though the trend leg can be mechanically driven by PPE shrinkage and thus partially proxy the known low-investment effect.

This is the same "expensive multiple × rising investment intensity" template already tested twice in the archive (PriceyGoodwillRollup, PriceyInventoryOverbuild), with only the investment proxy and the RANK→IND_RANK wrapper changed, so it is a cosmetic variant rather than a substantively different mechanism.

Direct rediscovery of the archived PriceyInventoryOverbuild — same MIN gate, same price-to-revenue leg, same inventory-intensity leg with DELTA swapped for TS_RANK and RANK swapped for IND_RANK — which is precisely the kind of cosmetic re-specification the objective warns against.

This is essentially the sign-mirrored twin of the archived PriceyGoodwillRollup (valuation crossed with intangible/goodwill accumulation), and the second leg is weakened by the fact that a falling intan/at often reflects routine amortization or asset-base growth rather than any deliberate restraint in intangible investment.

It overlaps the archived SalesValueHiringDiscipline and the published labor-hiring anomaly, but the employment-minus-sales growth gap is a genuinely different construct (deteriorating labor productivity rather than raw headcount growth) and the product-of-ranks orientation is internally consistent with the negative expected sign.

Algebraically the expression reduces to (ebitda × sale)/(3yr-capx × mktcap), so it is dominated by the 1/capx term and will be driven by near-zero-capex, asset-light firms (a sector/low-investment tilt already spanned by CMA) rather than by any genuine "capex payoff" mechanism, and a single 1% winsorization will not tame a ratio with a small, occasionally-zero denominator.

This is the third instance of the archive's MIN(IND_RANK(oancf/mktcap), IND_RANK(efficiency-improvement)) template (HarvestingCashFlowValue, CheapPredictableCapexYield), with only the second leg swapped, and it does nothing to address the diagnosed problem that the cash-flow-yield leg keeps producing positive FMB slopes alongside negative FF5 alphas.

The second leg is the exact sign-flipped construct already tested in CheapOrganicSalesNoAcquisition (aqc3/at vs. revenue growth), so this is largely a mirror-image rediscovery, and because a ~0–0.2 acquisition-to-assets ratio is differenced against a 3-year growth rate with far larger dispersion, the leg is in practice mostly negative revenue growth rather than M&A capital productivity.

The cash-deficit leg, (capx − oancf)/sale, is a genuinely different construct from the capex-trend and capex-volatility legs already tested and interacts coherently with the sales multiple, with the expected negative sign matching the expression's direction; the main caveat is substantial overlap with the documented external-financing/negative-FCF anomaly, which the test should control for.

This is a continuous restatement of the already-tested EbitdaValueMarginalPPEPayoff / PriceyCapitalProductivityFade family (value × growth-minus-capacity-growth gap) with sale substituted for ebitda, and the division by mktcap/sale makes magnitude explode for the cheapest firms so the ranking is dominated by the value leg rather than the operating-leverage idea.

Structurally identical to the archived PriceyCapitalProductivityFade — same MUL(IND_RANK(mktcap/sale), IND_RANK(NEG(TREND(productivity)))) template with only the productivity numerator/denominator and window changed — and the emp-based denominator is coarse and stale enough that a 3-point trend in oancf/emp is mostly noise.

The expression cleanly matches the hypothesis and the FCF-coverage leg is a substantive mechanism swap rather than a cosmetic tweak of CashValueCapexDecel, but the second leg is close to a plain free-cash-flow-margin/profitability characteristic, so incremental novelty over known FCF and cash-holdings anomalies is limited.

The inner product of two sign-flipping terms (Δinvt/sale × −oancf/sale) assigns high "stress" ranks both to inventory-building cash burners and to inventory-liquidating cash generators, so the computed quantity does not monotonically represent the hypothesized stress and repeats the exact flaw that made the archived PriceyLossMakingHiring and PriceyCashBurnAcquirer products weak.

Asset age (ppent/ppegt) is a genuinely new dimension for this archive, the expression is sign-consistent with the hypothesis, and the value×vintage interaction is economically motivated, though reviewers should note asset age is itself a documented investment-related characteristic so the incremental content must come from the conditioning.

It is essentially the archived PriceyLossMakingHiring with employee growth swapped for asset newness, and because ppent/ppegt only scales the magnitude of −ib/sale, profitable firms with newer capacity are pushed toward the "attractive" tail, contradicting the stated capacity-overpayment story.

Internally consistent and sensibly repositions the labor-productivity gap onto the cash-yield value leg that performed best in the archive, but the sales-minus-employment-growth leg is a near-restatement of the well-known hiring-rate anomaly already probed by two archived signals, so this is a moderate rather than large step.

A defensible extension of the strongest negative-side archive result toward funding strain, though the un-ranked sum of capex acceleration and cash change partly double-counts (capex mechanically drains cash) and misclassifies buyback/dividend-driven cash declines as distress, which risks diluting the signal.

The numerator subtracts a three-year-average flow (capx) from a balance-sheet stock (che), which is dimensionally incoherent and makes the construct essentially a cash-to-price value signal — itself a published anomaly (cash holdings/market cap) — with a small noisy tilt rather than the "capex claim on cash" mechanism claimed.

Internally consistent and sign-coherent, but it is essentially the archive's best signal (CashFundedCapexValue) with an inventory-release gate bolted on, so it is an incremental extension whose main risk is coverage attrition and unstable portfolio composition from a triple MIN.

The expression matches the hypothesis and sign, and the "is the cash borrowed from shareholders?" conditioning is economically sensible, though the second leg is a thin proxy for the well-known share-issuance anomaly, so the novelty rests entirely on the interaction rather than either component.

Monotonic construction is clean and the sign is correct, but this is largely PriceyCapexCashBurn re-cast as a MIN gate plus an external-financing leg that overlaps the established issuance/external-finance anomalies, and the triple gate on sparse sstk will likely shrink coverage below the already-low ~8%.

This is a cosmetic variant of the archived PriceyInventoryFundingStrain — identical first two legs with only the liquidity-strain proxy swapped from oancf/sale to Δche/at, a substitution already used in PriceyCapexCashDrawdown — so it tests no new economic mechanism.

Replacing the earlier sign-flipping product with a monotonic gate and swapping the earnings margin for operating cash flow is a defensible structural fix rather than pure cosmetics, but it recombines already-tested legs (rich sales multiple, employee growth, weak cash generation) and thus offers limited genuinely new information.

This is simply the MIN-intersection of two already-evaluated archive signals (CashCapexRunwayValue and CashValueNoDilution), introducing no new variable or mechanism while further shrinking coverage, so it is a redundant recombination rather than a test of a new idea.

Adding asset vintage to the already-tested CashFundedCapexValue gate is a coherent and internally consistent refinement of the harvesting mechanism, though the vintage leg previously produced wrong-signed FF5 alpha and the triple gate will push coverage below 0.08, so the incremental payoff is uncertain.

The acquisition-restraint channel is economically distinct from the capex/dilution conditioners already tested and the expression matches the stated sign, but the heavy mass of zero aqc means the conditioning leg ties at the top for most firms and the signal may largely degenerate into plain cash-to-price.

This uses exactly the same three ingredients as the archived PriceyCashBurnAcquirer with only the aggregation operator changed from product to MIN gate, a structure already demonstrated on the same cash-burn theme by PriceyHiringCashBurnGate, so it is close to a mechanical rediscovery rather than a new mechanism.

The expression is internally consistent and the debt-financing leg is a genuinely different funding channel from the archived equity-issuance version, but it is a single-ingredient swap that also overlaps substantially with the well-documented net-external-financing and asset-growth anomalies.

The asset-vintage leg (ppent/ppegt) is near-mechanically implied by sustained heavy capex, making it largely redundant with the capex-deficit leg, and this same vintage conditioner already produced a wrong-signed FF5 alpha in PriceyFreshCapacityUnderuse, so the expected negative sign is poorly supported.
This is the archive's CashFundedCapexValue with the after-capex margin merely three-year-summed — a smoothing tweak of the same two ingredients rather than a substantively different mechanism.

The construction is internally incoherent because subtracting aqc/at makes heavily acquisitive firms score as "restrained" even though acquisition-driven expansion predicts low returns, and the surviving content is largely the known asset-growth anomaly crossed with the already-tested cash-to-price leg.

Moving the archived CashCapexRunwayValue from a level to a bounded change is a defensible level-versus-improvement distinction, though the delta leg is mechanically correlated with cash accumulation and thus partly redundant with the che/price gate.
This is the archive's strongest short-side signal (PriceyCapexDeficitNoBuffer) with the deficit three-year-summed — a cosmetic smoothing variant using identical components and gating structure.

Aggregating capex and inventory build into a single monotonic cash-drain measure is a genuine structural change from the prior three-way MIN gates and avoids their coverage loss, though the underlying content overlaps the accrual/investment-financing literature.

This is a mechanical recombination of components already tested in PriceyHiringCashBurnGate and PriceyDilutiveCapexDeficit, and its two non-valuation legs are the well-documented employee-growth and net-equity-issuance anomalies.

This is essentially CheapPredictableCapexYield with the yield anchor swapped from oancf/P to che/P and the volatility window from 3 to 5 years — a cosmetic recombination of two already-tested legs, and the capex-volatility gate was the weakest component in the archive (ls_talpha -0.67).

A defensible broadening of the archive's strongest signal (CashValuePostCapexPeak) from fixed capital to total investment including working capital, though it is an incremental extension of a known winner and the signed DELTA(invt) term inside a TS_MAX peak comparison adds noise that may dilute rather than sharpen the harvest-phase identification.

Economically coherent and structurally distinct from prior gates (asset shrinkage conditioned on continued sales growth rather than capex-intensity change), but the NEG(GROWTH(ppent)) leg is close to the well-documented asset-growth/investment anomaly already spanned by FF5's CMA, which should temper alpha expectations.

This is the literal intersection of two already-evaluated signals (PriceyCapexDeficitNoBuffer and PriceyTotalInvestmentCashDrain), differing only by adding DELTA(invt) to the deficit numerator — a mechanical mashup rather than a new mechanism, and the triple MIN gate will further cut coverage below the already-thin 0.08.

Unlike the archive's change- and deficit-based short legs this uses levels (capex intensity and EBITDA margin), giving genuinely different portfolio composition, though the construct is close to the well-known expensive-plus-unprofitable "junk growth" interaction and both level legs are heavily industry-driven even after IND_RANK.

Swapping the weak-operating-cash leg of PriceyInventoryFundingStrain for equity issuance is a real change of mechanism (external financing of working capital rather than internal shortfall), but sstk-based gates have already been tested twice with inconsistent results and the signal will overlap substantially with the established net-share-issuance anomaly.

This is a cosmetic denominator tweak to the archive's CashCapexRunwayValue (adding positive-part inventory builds, an extension already explored in CashValueTotalInvestmentPeakExit), so it is very unlikely to deliver information beyond signals already tested.

The margin-improvement gate is a substantively different discriminator from the sales-growth gate that weakened NetCashCapexCutWithGrowth, and it directly addresses the "capex cut as distress" confound, though it remains within a heavily mined cash-value/capex-restraint family.

Internally inconsistent with its own rationale — since aqc/at minus its 5-year max is identically zero for firms that never acquire, never-acquirers receive the top gate score and are pooled with genuine peak-exiters, so the signal collapses toward the already-tested AcquisitionRestraintCashValue rather than distinguishing the two groups.

Changes-based reformulation of the weak levels-based PriceyCapexBurdenLowMargin is a defensible diagnosis-driven revision, and the MIN construction and expected negative sign are internally consistent.

Coherent demand-shortfall mechanism that substitutes a margin-change gate for the cash-flow-level gate in PriceyInventoryFundingStrain and rescues the failed PriceyInventoryOverbuild, with sign and construction internally consistent, though it is one of three near-identical templates submitted in this batch.

This is the third pass at "expensive firm hiring while profitability is weak" after PriceyLossMakingHiring and PriceyHiringCashBurnGate, differing only in which profitability proxy fills the same slot, so it is a cosmetic variant rather than a new mechanism.

This is essentially a merger of two already-tested archive winners (CashValuePostCapexPeak and CashValueCapexCutMarginGain) with MIN swapped for SUMRANK on the same two legs, so it is a cosmetic recombination rather than a new mechanism, and the redundant IND_RANK around a SUMRANK adds nothing.

The working-capital framing is a defensible sibling rather than a clone of the capex-peak family, but it substantially overlaps CashValueInventoryReleaseFCF (cash-value + inventory release + cash generation) with only a timing reparameterization (peak-relative level, cash-margin delta), and the triple hard gate will again thin coverage in a family already mined a dozen times.

This is CashValueTrueAcquisitionExit with the current-acquisition-restraint leg replaced by a SUMRANK that blends the same drop-from-peak term with a margin delta already used elsewhere, so it is an incremental reweighting of a tested signal rather than a substantively different hypothesis.

It stacks two already-tested and individually mediocre Pricey legs (PriceyTotalInvestmentCashDrain and the margin-erosion leg of PriceyCapexMarginErosion) via SUMRANK, which is a mechanical merge of weak evidence rather than a diagnosis of why the Pricey short leg keeps underdelivering.

This is the one proposal that poses a genuinely discriminating question — it deliberately reverses the capex-direction leg relative to PriceyCapexMarginErosion and to the cash-value harvest family, so the result will reveal whether the archive's signal is investment direction or simply deteriorating margins, though the reviewer should expect the margin leg to do most of the work.

DELTA(intan) is largely a non-cash accounting item driven by acquisition allocation and amortization, so adding it to a capex-minus-operating-cash-flow "cash drain" is internally inconsistent with the stated mechanism, and what remains is a thin variant of PriceyTotalInvestmentCashDrain.
